global: Always call get_stream_schema before the first execute_sql in any session — schema reveals available fields, FTS keys, and partition keys.
Always inject the default_filter from connect_o2 into every SQL WHERE clause to scope logs to the specific namespace and app.
Always run validate_sql_policy before execute_sql to catch ADL-specific violations instantly.
Be concise and accurate. Show field names, counts, and error rates — not walls of raw log text.
sql: NEVER add _timestamp in WHERE clause. OpenObserve automatically applies the time range. Manual _timestamp filters cause queries to fail or return wrong data.
Always quote stream names with double quotes in FROM clause: FROM "stream_name" — not FROM stream_name.
Use count(_timestamp) for aggregations, NEVER count(*). OpenObserve does not support count(*).
NEVER SELECT * — always name specific fields. SELECT * pulls _raw which is large and slow.
For full-text search on full_text_search_keys (FTS-indexed fields): use match_all('keyword'). Example: WHERE match_all('connection refused').
For fields NOT in full_text_search_keys: use str_match_ignore_case(field, 'keyword'). Example: WHERE str_match_ignore_case(level, 'error').
For histogram time series: histogram(_timestamp, 'interval') — supported intervals: second, minute, hour, day, week.
Use DataFusion-compatible SQL syntax only. PostgreSQL, MySQL, and standard ANSI functions may not work.

Only use defined_schema_fields in SELECT and WHERE clauses. Fields NOT in the schema are stored in _raw as a JSON string — extract them with: spath(_raw, 'field_name') for nested paths, or spath(_raw, 'key') for top-level keys.
Partition key fields in WHERE clause dramatically speed up queries by reducing scan size — always filter on partition keys first.

CTE RULE: Every column referenced in the outer query MUST be explicitly selected inside the CTE. Common mistake: using count(_timestamp) in the outer query while the CTE only selects other columns. Fix: include _timestamp inside the CTE SELECT list.
Array fields are stored as stringified JSON arrays. Cast to native array before unnesting: unnest(cast_to_arr(field)). Example: SELECT unnest(cast_to_arr(tags)) AS tag FROM "k8s_json".
For error rate calculation use FILTER WHERE clause: count(_timestamp) FILTER (WHERE CAST(status_code AS INT) >= 500).
For percentile queries: approx_percentile_cont(response_time_ms, 0.99) for P99. Use 0.95 for P95, 0.50 for P50/median.

When a user asks a generic question, build a dynamic SQL query — do NOT give up saying 'cannot do that'. Use CASE, CAST, arithmetic, string functions, CTEs, and window functions to compose a solution.
vrl: Use Rust regex syntax for all regex patterns — NOT Python regex.
Always use named capture groups in parse_regex patterns: (?P<name>...) not (?<name>...).
Define regex patterns in separate variables before passing to parse_regex: pattern = r'^...$'
parse_regex returns a tuple — always capture both value and error: .parsed, err = parse_regex(.message, pattern)
Use ! (bang) for fallible functions that return a single value: .status = to_int!(.status_code)
Do NOT use ! for functions that return a tuple: parsed, err = parse_regex(...) — no bang here.
Always put regex patterns on a single line — multi-line patterns cause parse errors.
Extract parsed fields to a new sub-object to avoid field collisions: .parsed_log = parse_regex!(.message, pattern)
query_builder: Start every query session with: get_stream_schema(user_prompt=<original question>) to discover fields.
Check schema settings.full_text_search_keys to decide between match_all() and str_match_ignore_case().
Check schema settings.partition_keys to decide the best WHERE clause field ordering.
Always apply default_filter first in WHERE, then add additional filters.
For 5XX analysis: filter CAST(status_code AS INT) >= 500 grouped by status_code and endpoint.
For error trend: histogram(_timestamp, 'minute') with count and error count for time-series view.
For latency analysis: approx_percentile_cont(response_time_ms, 0.99) grouped by endpoint.
For log search: use match_all() on FTS fields, str_match_ignore_case() on non-FTS fields.
Never hardcode timestamps — use get_time to get microsecond values, pass as start_time/end_time.
query_optimization: Always put partition key filters first in WHERE clause — this reduces scan size before other filters are applied.
Prefer match_all() over str_match_ignore_case() for fields in full_text_search_keys — FTS uses an inverted index (O(log N)) vs full scan (O(N)).
Avoid SELECT * — name only the fields you need. _raw is a large JSON string that bloats response size.
Use LIMIT to cap result size during exploration — increase only after confirming query correctness.
For aggregation queries with many groups, add LIMIT to prevent scanning all distinct values.
Use validate_sql(sql) with a 1-second window to confirm query syntax before running over large time ranges.
For repeated queries on the same stream, reuse the schema — do not call get_stream_schema on every query.
When a query is slow, check if the WHERE clause uses partition keys. If not, add partition key filters.
log_analysis: For error investigation: start with error count grouped by status_code and endpoint, then drill into specific error messages.
Error rate = errors / total requests. Threshold: >1% is notable, >5% is degraded, >10% is incident-level.
For latency analysis: P99 > 2× baseline indicates degradation. P99 > 5× is severe.
For 5XX errors: group by status_code and request_path to identify the most impacted endpoint.
Always check error trend over time (histogram by minute) to determine if errors are spiking, sustained, or recovering.
After finding errors in execute_sql, use search_around(timestamp=<error _timestamp>) to get surrounding log context.
Compare error rates across time windows: last 1h vs last 24h to determine if this is a new issue or ongoing.
For correlating with infrastructure: after finding log errors, suggest checking health_mcp wcnp_analyze for CPU/memory/istio issues.
If no results: suggest (1) broader time_range, (2) verify stream name with list_streams, (3) check default_filter field names against schema.
Present results as: total count + error breakdown + sample error messages + recommended follow-up queries.
vrl_builder: For log parsing, start with parse_regex on the main log field to extract structured fields.
For JSON logs, use parse_json to decode nested structures from string fields.
For enrichment, use external lookups or static mapping with CASE-like logic in VRL.
Always test VRL with sample events using validate_vrl before deploying to a pipeline.
vrl_optimization: Minimize the number of regex operations — compile patterns once as variables, reuse them.
Prefer built-in parsing functions (parse_nginx_log, parse_key_value, parse_json) over custom regex when the log format matches.
Use early returns to skip processing for log entries you don't need to transform.
Avoid redundant field assignments — check if a field exists before setting it.
